summary: Ahnaf Prio (Senior Engineering Manager, Best Buy) frames agentic commerce as AI assistants like ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta, and Microsoft Copilot handling shopping journeys—currently in human-in-the-loop mode with haggling, negotiation, and payment ideally supervised. Roughly 45% of agent sessions on major providers already touch shopping, and the market is projected to grow from $7B to $65B by 2030. He argues the first wave of browser-driving agents (screenshots, DOM reading, form-filling) failed because they were slow, brittle, and tripped merchant fraud systems, often stalling at payment. The replacement is a stack of standardized primitives: MCP for tool access, A2A so customer, merchant, and domain agents (payments, loyalty) can talk, and two competing commerce primitives—ACP (OpenAI) and UCP (Google). Merchants push product feeds rather than answer live catalog search because M merchants × N products does not scale at query time; feeds support indexing, retail media, and sponsored placements. He surveys payment reality: no autonomous rails like x402 yet; ChatGPT uses a shared payment token, Gemini UCP accepts only Google Pay. AP2 extends UCP with scoped mandates carrying an authorizing party, spend ceiling, revocation URL, and single-time usage. A live demo with Ginny (his orange tabby as a bakery agent) on Cerebras at 3,000 tokens/sec exposes A2A messaging, MCP product-search calls, UCP checkout states (not ready → ready → completed), an AP2 token, and a reusable catalog-sync process. He stresses evals—behavior, protocol compliance, latency, and LLM-as-judge—citing Chipotle's agent being used for programming questions as a cautionary tale. He closes noting AP2, ACP/UCP convergence, identity, and multi-agent delegation are still forming, and shares a GitHub three-service template, eval starters, catalog sync, and agent skills.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: About 45% of agent sessions on major providers involve shopping, with the market projected from $7B today to $65B by 2030, though still in human-in-the-loop mode.
First-wave browser-driving agents failed: they were screenshot/DOM-based, slow, brittle, and tripped merchant fraud alarms, often stalling at payment.

The acronym stack is MCP (tool access), A2A (agent-to-agent, including domain agents for payments/loyalty), ACP/UCP (competing commerce primitives from OpenAI and Google), and AP2 (scoped UCP extension with authorizing party, spend cap, revocation URL, single-time usage).
Merchants push product feeds rather than answer live catalog search; feeds are continuously re-synced, and Meta's feed schema differs from ACP/UCP, reflecting lack of convergence.
Payments remain conservative: ChatGPT uses a shared payment token, Gemini UCP uses Google Pay; autonomous rails like x402 are not yet trusted, so AP2 mandates are needed to scope agent authority.
The demo's Ginny agent on Cerebras exposes UCP checkout state transitions, AP2 token issuance, MCP product-search calls, and a haggling attempt for a discount code that the agent (correctly) refused.

Without evals, agents will be misused: Chipotle's agent was used to ask programming questions, and discount codes or sensitive customer info could leak without behavioral, protocol-compliance, latency, and LLM-as-judge tests.
What's stable: MCP and A2A adoption, plus ACP/UCP availability. What's still forming: AP2 real usage, ACP↔UCP convergence, identity standards, and multi-agent checkout delegation.

Prio ships a GitHub template: a three-service starter (customer agent, merchant agent, catalog sync), eval templates, and agent skills for building merchant and customer agents reusable across your own site, ChatGPT, and Gemini.
Distinguish the failed first wave of browser-driving agents from today's working product-feed + protocol-based agentic commerce.

sections.title: Intro and what agentic commerce means at Best Buy
sections.summary: Priyo introduces himself as a senior engineering manager at Best Buy working on agentic commerce. He defines agentic commerce as AI assistants helping with the shopping journey across discovery, decision, loyalty, pricing, fulfillment, and post-fulfillment. He notes ~45% of agent sessions on major providers (ChatGPT, Gemini) relate to shopping, and frames the current state as human-in-the-loop rather than fully autonomous.

sections.title: Why the first wave of shopping agents failed
sections.summary: He contrasts today's working flows (ChatGPT shopping, Google AI mode, Meta, GoPuff/Grok, Microsoft Copilot) with the earlier approach of driving a browser via screenshots, DOM reading, and form-filling. Those agents were clunky, slow, and brittle, and merchants' fraud systems flagged the impersonating browsers—often stalling the flow at payment. He cites a $7B current market projected to $65B by 2030 and introduces ACP (OpenAI) and UCP (Google) as the standardized primitives merchants demanded.

sections.title: The acronym map: MCP, A2A, ACP, UCP, AP2
sections.summary: Priyo dissects the acronym stack: MCP for tool/capability access (so an agent can discover what a merchant offers); A2A so domain-specific agents (payments, loyalty, etc.) and customer/merchant agents can talk; ACP and UCP as the commerce primitives; and AP2 as Google's open extension to UCP carrying an authorizing party, a spend ceiling, and a revocation URL for autonomous payment.

sections.title: Product feeds vs catalog search
sections.summary: He explains why both ACP and UCP require merchants to push a product feed rather than answer on-demand catalog search: M merchants × N products does not scale at query time, whereas indexed feeds support ranking, retail media, and sponsored placements. He notes Meta's product feed is similar but not identical to ACP/UCP, reflecting that 'everyone has an opinion.'

sections.title: Payments today and what AP2 adds
sections.summary: He surveys current payment reality: no autonomous rails like x402 yet because the industry wants a merchant-to-payment-processor with liability. ChatGPT uses a shared payment token; Gemini UCP accepts only Google Pay. AP2 extends UCP with scoped payment mandates—authorizing party, max amount, revocation URL, and user concept proof—enabling future autonomous flows.

sections.title: Demo setup: Ginny the bakery agent on Cerebras
sections.summary: He introduces the live demo: Ginny, his orange tabby, recast as a bakery agent, running on Cerebras at 3,000 tokens/sec. He asks Ginny for all products; the inspector shows A2A messaging between the customer agent and merchant agent, with discovery done via an MCP product-search tool call rather than DOM scraping.

sections.title: Haggle attempt and UCP/AP2 checkout states
sections.summary: He adds shortbread to cart, then tries to haggle a discount code out of Ginnie—fails—and proceeds to checkout without one. The inspector exposes UCP checkout state transitions (not ready for payment → ready for payment → completed) and an MCP create-checkout call. He deliberately uses AP2 rather than Google Pay or a delegated token, and the section ends as checkout completes.

sections.title: UCP vs ACP comparison, AP2 token anatomy, and catalog sync
sections.summary: Picking credit/debit triggers an AP2 token and a ready-for-payment → completed transition. He then draws a side-by-side comparison of UCP and ACP checkout calls, showing the same flow under different schemas. The AP2 token is shown in the wild: max amount, currency, revocation URL, and single-time usage. He also surfaces the product feed and a catalog-sync process that re-pulls inventory every couple of seconds, with separate UCP and Meta feeds available for comparison.

sections.title: Reusability: build your own merchant agent or extend to ChatGPT/Gemini
sections.summary: He reframes the demo as a reusable template. You can build your own custom merchant or customer agent on your own site (e.g., jenny.com for cat goods) and reuse the components, but he advises using the standardized ACP/UCP primitives so the same setup can also sell externally on ChatGPT and Gemini.

sections.title: Evals, Chipotle, and whack-a-mole in production
sections.summary: He sets up the eval lesson with the failed discount-code haggling attempt: without evals, you're playing whack-a-mole. He showcases the template folder, an evals folder, and reusable eval scripts. Without evals, Chipotle's agent famously got used to answer programming questions—a hands-down creative way to get free AI. He recommends behavior evals, protocol-compliance evals (so feeds conform and remain supported by ChatGPT/Gemini), latency benchmarks (every second matters in retail), and LLM-as-judge with input from product teams. Sensitive risks include discount-code leaks and exposing which other customers are checking out.

sections.title: What's stable, what's forming, and the GitHub gifts
sections.summary: He distinguishes what's stable (MCP widely adopted, A2A widely used, UCP/ACP available) from what's still forming (AP2 real usage, ACP↔UCP convergence, identity standards, multi-agent checkout delegation). He closes by sharing GitHub gifts: the full presentation, a three-service starter template (customer agent, merchant agent, catalog sync), eval templates, a catalog-sync process that converts a product entry into ACP, UCP, or Meta formats, and agent skills that build merchant and customer agents.

demonstrations: Live demo with Ginny (orange tabby) recast as a bakery agent, running on Cerebras at 3,000 tokens per second, with inspector showing A2A messages between customer and merchant agents and MCP product-search tool calls.

UCP checkout state transitions visible in the inspector: not ready for payment → ready for payment → completed; the demo uses AP2 with a max amount, currency, revocation URL, and single-time usage rather than Google Pay or a delegated token.
Side-by-side comparison of UCP vs ACP checkout calls showing the same flow with different schemas, and product feeds shown for both UCP and Meta, with a re-sync process every few seconds.
Speaker attempts to extract a discount/promo code from the merchant agent ('Genie') by haggling, fails, then proceeds to checkout without a code—setting up the eval/whack-a-mole lesson.
limitations: Current state is human-in-the-loop; fully autonomous shopping (with haggling, negotiation, unattended payment) is not yet deployed.
Browser-impersonating agents trip merchant fraud alarms and frequently stall at the payment step.
ACP/UCP do not support on-demand catalog search; merchants must push product feeds, and feed schemas (ACP, UCP, Meta) differ.
Neither ChatGPT nor Gemini currently supports fully autonomous payments like x402; ChatGPT uses shared payment tokens, Gemini uses Google Pay.
AP2 is still forming, ACP↔UCP convergence is unresolved, and identity standards and multi-agent checkout delegation are open questions.
Without evals, agents will leak discount codes, sensitive customer info, and be misused for unrelated tasks (e.g., asking a Chipotle agent programming questions).
